A current account surplus means the economy is a net lender to the world; deficit means net borrower. (2) Capital & Financial Account — capital transfers (e.g. debt forgiveness) and financial transactions: direct investment (FDI), portfolio investment, financial derivatives, reserve assets. (3) Net Errors & Omissions — balancing item. By double-entry bookkeeping, BoP always balances: Current Account + Capital & Financial Account + Net Errors & Omissions = 0. A current account deficit must be financed by a financial account surplus (capital inflow). Exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. HKD uses a linked exchange rate system: USD/HKD fixed at 7.80 (band 7.75–7.85), backed by US dollar reserves. Under the Convertibility Undertakings, the HKMA buys US dollars from banks at 7.75 (strong-side, when the Hong Kong dollar is strong) and sells US dollars to banks at 7.85 (weak-side, when the Hong Kong dollar is weak). 7.80 is the anchor inside the band, not itself a convertibility rate. Market forces keep the rate within the band. Appreciation (stronger currency) makes exports dearer, imports cheaper — worsens trade balance; depreciation does the opposite. Real exchange rate = nominal rate × (domestic price level / foreign price level) — reflects true competitiveness. Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) theory: in the long run, exchange rates adjust to equalise price levels across countries. The J-curve effect: after a depreciation, the trade balance may worsen before improving because import/export volumes adjust slowly. Marshall-Lerner condition: depreciation improves the trade balance only if the sum of export and import demand elasticities exceeds 1. In HK's linked rate system, nominal exchange rate stability means competitiveness adjusts through domestic prices and wages (internal devaluation).

example.scenario: A Hong Kong logistics firm exports HK$500 million of freight services to the US, imports HK$200 million of fuel, receives HK$50 million in investment income from overseas subsidiaries, and its parent company in the UK invests HK$300 million in new warehouses in HK.
example.walkthrough: Step 1: Record in Current Account. Exports of services: +HK$500m (credit). Imports of goods (fuel): -HK$200m (debit). Primary income (investment income received): +HK$50m (credit). Current Account balance = +500 - 200 + 50 = +HK$350m surplus. Step 2: Record in Financial Account. UK parent's FDI in HK warehouses: +HK$300m (credit, inflow). Assume no other financial flows. Financial Account balance = +HK$300m surplus. Step 3: Check BoP identity — Current Account (+350) + Financial Account (+300) = +650. This cannot be; there must be offsetting outflows. Step 4: Find the missing entry — the firm pays for fuel imports by drawing down its USD bank deposits abroad (financial account debit -HK$200m), and the HK$500m service export is paid by US clients depositing USD in HK banks (financial account credit +HK$500m). Revised Financial Account: +300 (FDI) -200 (deposit drawdown) +500 (deposit inflow) = +600. Step 5: Net Errors & Omissions = -HK$250m to balance. Step 6: Exchange rate context — under linked rate, USD inflows expand Aggregate Balance, putting downward pressure on HIBOR; HKMA may need to sell HKD/buy USD to keep rate at 7.80.

traps: Students think a current account deficit is 'bad' and surplus 'good'; a deficit can reflect high investment (capital inflow) which raises future capacity, while a surplus may indicate weak domestic demand.
Students confuse the financial account with the capital account; the capital account covers capital transfers (small), while the financial account covers investment flows (large).
Students assume the exchange rate is always floating; HK's linked rate means the nominal USD/HKD rate is fixed, so competitiveness adjusts via domestic prices/wages, not the exchange rate.

Students forget double-entry bookkeeping: every transaction has a credit and debit entry of equal value, so the BoP always balances overall — a current account deficit implies a financial account surplus.

terms.definition: A systematic record of all economic transactions between residents of an economy and the rest of the world in a given period.
Records trade in goods and services, primary income (wages, investment income) and secondary income (transfers).
Records cross-border financial transactions: direct investment, portfolio investment, derivatives, and reserve assets.
A currency board arrangement where HKD is pegged to USD at 7.80, fully backed by USD reserves, with convertibility undertakings at 7.75 and 7.80.
Appreciation: currency becomes stronger (fewer units per foreign currency); depreciation: currency becomes weaker.
Nominal exchange rate adjusted for price level differences; measures true international competitiveness.

L1.4.title: Scarcity, Opportunity Cost, and the Law of Supply
L1.4.concept: Demand and supply sit on two ideas the diagram does not draw. Scarcity means wants exceed the resources available, so a choice is required. The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next best alternative forgone — not the sum of every alternative, and not the money price unless that price is being used as a measure of what was given up. A free good has zero opportunity cost; an economic good does not. The law of supply states that, ceteris paribus, a higher price leads to a higher quantity supplied, so the supply curve slopes upward. To produce more, firms pull resources away from other uses, and those uses become more valuable at the margin, so a higher price is needed to call forth extra output. A change in the good's own price moves the firm along the supply curve. A non-price change shifts the curve: input prices, technology, the number of sellers, expectations, taxes and subsidies, the price of an alternative output, and, for farm goods, weather. This note follows the usual HKDSE treatment; the current curriculum guide on the HKEAA website is the authority for wording and scope.

example.scenario: A cha chaan teng can use the same kitchen hour to fry egg tarts or to serve milk tea. The price of egg tarts rises. Flour prices and the price of milk tea stay the same at first.
example.walkthrough: The opportunity cost of the egg tarts is the milk tea given up, if that is the next best use of the hour — not the sum of every other dish, and not the sticker price of an egg tart. The higher egg-tart price makes it worth sacrificing more milk tea, so quantity supplied of egg tarts rises. That is a movement along the supply curve. If flour then becomes more expensive, cost is higher at every price and the supply curve shifts left. If instead the price of milk tea rises, the kitchen switches toward milk tea and egg-tart supply shifts left, because the opportunity cost of egg tarts has increased.

traps: Treating opportunity cost as the sum of all forgone options. Only the single next-best alternative counts.
Calling the money price the opportunity cost whenever the question asks what was given up.
Saying supply falls when the good's own price falls. Quantity supplied contracts along the curve.
Treating a per-unit subsidy as a demand shift. It lowers producers' costs and shifts supply rightward (downward on the diagram).
Drawing a downward-sloping supply curve to mirror demand. The usual HKDSE supply curve slopes upward.

terms.definition: A situation in which wants exceed the resources available to satisfy them, so choice is required.
The value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made.
A good with zero opportunity cost. An economic good has a positive opportunity cost.
Ceteris paribus, a higher price leads to a higher quantity supplied.
The amount producers are willing and able to sell at one price; a point on the supply curve.

L2.3.title: How to Answer an Elasticity Question
L2.3.concept: Elasticity questions are mostly a fixed routine. Step 1: name the elasticity and write the formula with the right variables. PED uses the good's own price, YED uses income, XED uses the other good's price, and PES uses quantity supplied. Step 2: calculate percentage changes from the original values unless the question says otherwise, and keep the sign. Step 3: classify in a full sentence. For PED and PES, use the absolute value: greater than 1 is elastic, less than 1 is inelastic, and 1 is unitary. For YED and XED, the sign is the classification: positive YED means a normal good (above 1, a luxury; between 0 and 1, a necessity), negative YED means an inferior good; positive XED means substitutes, negative XED means complements. Step 4: state one consequence the number actually supports — total revenue, the type of good, or the effect of time on PES — and stop. Do not call a curve elastic because it looks flat. Elasticity uses percentages. Formula details follow the current HKEAA curriculum guide.

example.scenario: The price of a ticket rises from $20 to $25 and the quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80. Income is unchanged. A student reports PED as 0.8 and says total revenue falls.
example.walkthrough: Percentage change in price = 5/20 × 100% = +25%. Percentage change in quantity demanded = −20/100 × 100% = −20%. PED = −20% / +25% = −0.8. The signed answer is −0.8; 0.8 is the absolute value. Because |PED| = 0.8 < 1, demand is price-inelastic. An inelastic demand curve and a higher price mean total revenue rises, because the percentage rise in price exceeds the percentage fall in quantity. The student's revenue conclusion contradicts the classification. Using 25 or the average as the base would be a different method, and only if the question asks for it.

traps: Using the new price as the base when the question expects the change relative to the original value.
Reporting PED as a positive 0.8. The ratio is negative; 0.8 is |PED|.
Calling YED > 1 'price-elastic demand'. That label belongs to PED. YED > 1 means a luxury.
Letting the revenue sentence contradict the class. Inelastic demand plus a higher price raises total revenue.
Putting good A's own price in the denominator of XED. XED uses the other good's price.

terms.definition: Percentage changes measured from the starting price or quantity, unless the question specifies another base.
|PED|, used only to classify elastic, inelastic, or unitary demand. The calculated PED itself is negative.
If |PED| < 1, price and total revenue move in the same direction. If |PED| > 1, they move in opposite directions.

L3.3.title: Externalities and Public Goods
L3.3.concept: Intervention is easier to explain when the market quantity is not the socially efficient quantity. With no externality, a competitive market settles where marginal private benefit equals marginal private cost. A negative production externality — for example, untreated wastewater — means marginal social cost is above marginal private cost. The firm ignores the external cost, produces more than the socially efficient quantity, and a deadweight loss appears. A per-unit tax equal to the external cost at the social optimum shifts supply left toward that quantity. A positive externality — for example, a vaccination that also protects other people — means marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit, so the market quantity is too low and a subsidy can close the gap. A public good is both non-rival (one person's use does not reduce another's) and non-excludable (non-payers are hard to keep out). Street lighting is the usual example. Private firms tend to underprovide it because of free riders. A merit good is different: education can be rival and excludable, and a subsidy is argued from external benefits or poor information, not from the public-good test. Scope follows the current HKEAA curriculum guide.

example.scenario: A factory sells plastic parts in a competitive market and dumps untreated wastewater into a typhoon shelter. Residents bear a cost that rises with the factory's output.
example.walkthrough: Buyers and the factory see only the private cost, so output settles where marginal private benefit equals marginal private cost. Marginal social cost lies above marginal private cost. The socially efficient output is the smaller quantity where marginal private benefit equals marginal social cost. A per-unit tax can shift supply left toward that quantity. The tax does not remove scarcity; it makes the firm count a cost it was imposing on others. A price ceiling would not target the external cost and could add a shortage. The parts are not a public good: they are rival and excludable. The clean public-good example in the same town would be lighting on the public pier.

traps: Calling every government-funded service a public good. A clinic visit can be rival and excludable.
Shifting demand for a production externality. A negative production externality is a gap between marginal social cost and marginal private cost.
Saying the free market always overproduces. Positive externalities mean too little is produced.
Describing only one feature of a public good. Both non-rivalry and non-excludability are required.
Using a price ceiling as if it were a corrective tax. The ceiling does not charge the external cost.

terms.definition: A cost imposed on third parties, so marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost and the market quantity is too high.
A benefit to third parties, so marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit and the market quantity is too low.
A good that is both non-rival and non-excludable, so private firms tend to underprovide it.
Someone who enjoys a non-excludable good without paying, which undermines private provision.
A good the government may subsidise because of external benefits or information problems. It need not be a public good.

L4.3.title: Division of Labour and Types of Production
L4.3.concept: Division of labour means splitting production into separate tasks so each worker specialises. Output per worker can rise because the task is repeated, less time is lost switching tools, and specialised tools become worth using. The costs are boredom, dependence on other workers, and a narrower skill that is harder to transfer if the industry shrinks — a later link to structural unemployment. Division of labour is not economies of scale. A small shop can divide tasks, whereas economies of scale are a fall in long-run average cost as the firm's scale of output grows. Types of production describe the stage. Primary production extracts natural resources, such as fishing or farming. Secondary production manufactures or constructs. Tertiary production supplies services such as retail, transport, finance, and education. Hong Kong's employment is concentrated in tertiary production, but the city still uses primary and secondary output produced elsewhere. Services are output and are counted in GDP when they are currently produced. These notes follow the usual HKDSE treatment; the curriculum guide on the HKEAA website sets the scope.

example.scenario: A noodle shop moves from one cook doing everything to three roles: one folds dumplings, one tends the wok, and one takes payment. Later it opens three branches and buys flour more cheaply in bulk.
example.walkthrough: The three roles are division of labour inside one shop, not yet a change of scale. Dumpling output per morning can rise because that cook stops walking to the till. Boredom and a stalled morning if the wok cook is absent are the costs. Opening branches and buying flour more cheaply is a separate idea: economies of scale, a fall in long-run average cost as scale grows. The meal sold to diners is tertiary production even though the dumplings are physical. A farm that only grows the wheat is primary. A factory that packs frozen dumplings is secondary.

traps: Using 'economies of scale' for any gain from specialisation. Specialisation can happen in a small firm.
Treating money as a factor of production. Capital means man-made aids such as ovens and tools.
Calling a restaurant primary production because it uses food. The output it sells is a service.
Listing only the advantages of division of labour when the question asks for effects.
Treating services as if they were not production. Tertiary output is counted in GDP when currently produced.

terms.definition: Splitting production into specialised tasks. It can raise output per worker and also creates dependence and narrower skills.
Concentrating on a narrow task or product in which practice and suitable tools raise productivity.
Extracting natural resources, such as farming, fishing, or mining.
Manufacturing or construction that transforms materials into goods.
The production of services, such as retail, transport, finance, and education.

L5.3.title: Monopolistic Competition and a Comparison Checklist
L5.3.concept: Between perfect competition and monopoly, answers usually need two further labels. Monopolistic competition has many firms, free entry, and differentiated products (brand, location, or quality). Each firm has limited price-making power, so its demand curve slopes down, but it is flatter than a monopolist's because substitutes are close. Short-run economic profit is possible. Free entry then shifts each firm's demand left until long-run profit is normal. The firm does not produce at the lowest point of its average-cost curve; textbooks call that excess capacity. It does not mean the firm is making a loss. Oligopoly, named in the previous lesson, has a few interdependent firms: a price cut may be matched, so competition often shifts to advertising, service, or features. Collusion can raise joint profit and is unstable if one firm gains by secretly cutting price. Before you name a structure, check four rows: number of firms, product, barriers, and long-run profit. A street of small cafés is a classroom illustration of monopolistic competition, not a legal finding. How much diagram work is required depends on the current curriculum guide.

example.scenario: Two new coffee shops open on the same street. Each has its own name and a slightly different drink list. A year later neither earns economic profit, but both still advertise.
example.walkthrough: Many sellers, differentiated drinks, and no serious barrier to a small shop fit monopolistic competition better than monopoly or perfect competition. Early profit would attract the second shop; free entry pushes long-run economic profit toward normal. Advertising can continue because the products are not identical. Excess capacity can remain: each shop may operate above the lowest possible average cost even though profit is only normal. If instead three chains supplied almost all of the packaged coffee on the street and each watched the others' prices, interdependence would make oligopoly the better label. One shop's slogan is not evidence about the whole market.

traps: Calling any brand an oligopoly. Many differentiated sellers with free entry are monopolistic competition.
Saying monopolistic competition earns economic profit forever. Free entry competes long-run profit down to normal.
Treating excess capacity as proof of losses. It means output is below the average-cost minimum.
Assuming oligopolists can never change price. Interdependence makes a price cut risky; it does not forbid one.
Judging the market from one firm's advertising line. Use the four-row checklist.

terms.definition: Many firms, differentiated products, and free entry. Long-run economic profit tends to be normal, with some price-making power.
Differences in brand, quality, or location that give a firm a downward-sloping demand curve.
Output below the level that minimises average cost. It can occur while economic profit is normal.
A few interdependent firms. Each must consider how rivals react to price or output decisions.
Competition on advertising, service, or features, common when matching price cuts is risky.

L6.3.title: Aggregate Demand and Short-run Aggregate Supply
L6.3.concept: Questions about the price level or real output need aggregate demand (AD) and short-run aggregate supply (SRAS), not the demand curve for one good. Put the price level on the vertical axis and real output on the horizontal axis. AD is planned spending on domestic final output, C + I + G + X − M. It slopes downward in the usual teaching account: a higher price level reduces the real value of money balances, raises interest rates and so reduces interest-sensitive spending, and makes domestic goods less competitive against foreign goods. A change in the price level is a movement along AD. A change in C, I, G, or net exports at a given price level shifts AD. SRAS slopes upward because some input costs are slow to change, so a higher price level raises profitability and firms produce more. Short-run equilibrium is the intersection. AD shifting right along a given SRAS raises both real output and the price level (demand-pull). SRAS shifting left raises the price level and lowers real output (cost-push). Hong Kong is a small open economy, so part of any rise in spending leaks into imports and does not raise demand for domestic output. The curriculum guide states how much of this mechanism is required.

example.scenario: A cut in salaries tax leaves government spending unchanged. Households spend part of the extra disposable income on local meals and part on imported phones.
example.walkthrough: The tax cut raises disposable income. Spending on local meals increases demand for domestic output, so AD shifts right. Spending on imported phones raises imports and offsets part of that shift, which is why an open-economy multiplier is smaller than a simple closed-economy one. Along the original SRAS, equilibrium real output and the price level both rise. This is not a movement along the demand curve for one meal. If restaurants later pay higher wages and those wages stay up, SRAS can shift left in a separate step. You cannot read the new price level from AD alone.

traps: Using a single-good demand-and-supply diagram to explain the general price level.
Saying a higher price level shifts AD left. That change is a movement along AD.
Treating every rise in the price level as demand-pull. A leftward SRAS shift raises the price level while real output falls.
Ignoring imports when consumption rises. Imported goods are a leakage from demand for domestic output.
Quoting one multiplier for every economy. Saving, tax, and imports all change its size.

terms.definition: Planned spending on domestic final output: C + I + G + X − M, drawn against the price level.
The relationship between the price level and real output when some input costs have not yet fully adjusted.
A change in the quantity of real output demanded caused only by a change in the price level.
A rightward shift of AD that raises both the price level and real output along a given SRAS.
A leftward shift of SRAS that raises the price level and reduces real output.

L10.3.title: Tariffs and the Limits of Protection
L10.3.concept: A tariff is a tax on imports. Where the good is also produced at home, a tariff raises the domestic price toward the world price plus the tariff, reduces imports, and raises the quantity supplied by domestic producers. The government collects tariff revenue on the units that are still imported, not on domestic output. Consumers lose on the units they still buy; domestic producers gain. The standard diagram has a deadweight loss because some purchases worth more than the world price no longer happen, and some domestic output costs more to produce than the good would have cost to import. A quota, already compared with taxes in the intervention unit, can also raise the domestic price, but the gap between the domestic price and the world price is quota rent for licence holders unless the licences are auctioned. Arguments for protection should be stated as arguments, not slogans: an infant industry may need time to gain scale, or a good may be treated as strategic. Arguments against include higher prices, retaliation, and the loss of gains from specialisation. A tariff changes prices and quantities; it does not rewrite opportunity-cost ratios or create comparative advantage. Whether a question expects the full surplus diagram depends on the current curriculum guide.

example.scenario: Bottled juice is imported at a world price of $10. A $4 tariff is imposed, the domestic price rises to $14, local bottlers produce more, and fewer bottles are imported.
example.walkthrough: The tariff is a wedge of $4 between the world price and the domestic price. Local bottlers move up their supply curve, so domestic quantity supplied rises. Buyers move up their demand curve, so quantity demanded falls. Imports are the gap between domestic demand and domestic supply, and that gap shrinks. Tariff revenue is $4 times the number of bottles still imported. It is not $4 times local production. Consumers pay $14 on every bottle they still buy, including local bottles. The revenue rectangle is a transfer to the government. The deadweight loss is the trades that no longer happen, not that rectangle. A quota that cut imports by the same amount need not give the government this revenue.

traps: Charging tariff revenue on domestic output. Revenue is collected only on imports that still enter.
Saying a tariff shifts the demand curve. The usual diagram is a wedge between the world price and the domestic price.
Treating a quota and a tariff as identical in every respect. A quota need not raise government revenue.
Counting 'protects jobs' as a free gain. Buyers pay a higher price, and that belongs in the answer.
Claiming a tariff creates comparative advantage. Comparative advantage is about opportunity cost.

terms.definition: A tax on imports. It raises the domestic price above the world price by up to the amount of the tax.
Tariff per unit multiplied by the quantity still imported.
The loss of surplus from trades that no longer happen: higher-cost domestic output and foregone consumption.
The premium earned by holders of import licences when a quota drives the domestic price above the world price.
An argument for temporary protection so a new industry can gain scale. It is an argument, not a result that always follows.

L7.3.title: Costs of Inflation and Deflation
L7.3.concept: Inflation is costly even when the CPI rise is moderate, and the costs depend on whether the rise was expected. Unanticipated inflation redistributes real income. Borrowers gain and lenders lose if the loan's nominal interest rate was fixed before prices rose, and people on fixed nominal incomes lose purchasing power. Once inflation is anticipated, contracts can build in a higher nominal interest rate, so that redistribution is smaller. The real interest rate is approximately the nominal rate minus expected inflation. Anticipated inflation still has costs. Menu costs are the real resources used to change listed prices. Shoe-leather costs are the time and effort spent economising on money balances because money loses purchasing power. Uncertainty about future prices makes long-term contracts and investment harder to plan. In Hong Kong, a rise in local costs while the exchange rate is held inside the currency-board band can also weaken price competitiveness against economies whose costs rise more slowly, because the Hong Kong dollar does not float freely to offset that gap. Deflation, a sustained fall in the general price level, is not a free gain. It raises the real burden of fixed nominal debts, can delay spending if people expect further price falls, and can raise real wages if nominal wages are sticky. A one-off change in a single price is still not inflation or deflation. These notes follow the usual HKDSE treatment; the curriculum guide sets what a question can require.

example.scenario: A Hong Kong household borrowed $2,000,000 at a fixed mortgage rate of 3% before an unexpected year in which the CPI rose by 6%. A restaurant on the same estate reprinted its price list four times. A saver who had expected the 6% rise negotiated a higher deposit rate.
example.walkthrough: The mortgage repayment is fixed in dollars, so the 6% rise in the price level cuts the real burden of the debt. The household gains and the lender loses because the inflation was not built into the 3% rate. The real interest rate on that loan is about 3% minus 6%, which is negative. The restaurant's reprinting is a menu cost: real resources used to change listed prices. If customers make extra trips to the bank to keep less cash, that time is a shoe-leather cost. The saver who expected 6% inflation and obtained a higher nominal deposit rate has protected the expected real return. That is anticipated inflation, not a gift to the borrower. None of these effects is a change in the linked rate. The currency board still holds the Hong Kong dollar inside the convertibility zone.

traps: Treating every cost of inflation as a redistribution. Menu costs, shoe-leather costs, and planning uncertainty remain even when inflation is anticipated.
Saying the real interest rate equals the nominal rate. Approximately, real rate = nominal rate minus expected inflation.
Calling a fall in one good's price deflation. Deflation is a sustained fall in the general price level.
Claiming deflation always helps debtors. A fixed nominal debt becomes heavier in real terms when the price level falls.
Using the linked exchange rate as if a rise in Hong Kong costs were automatically offset by a floating HKD. Under the currency board the rate stays inside the band.

terms.definition: A rise in the price level that was not expected when nominal contracts were set, so it redistributes real income.
A rise in the price level that people expected, so nominal interest rates and other contracts can adjust in advance.
Approximately the nominal interest rate minus the expected inflation rate. It measures the expected change in purchasing power.
The real cost of changing listed prices when the price level is changing.
A sustained fall in the general price level. It raises the real burden of fixed nominal debts.

L7.4.title: Natural Rate, the Phillips Curve, and Measurement Pitfalls
L7.4.concept: The unemployment rate is not one problem. Frictional unemployment is time spent matching workers to jobs. Structural unemployment is a mismatch of skills or location, often after an industry shrinks. Together they make up the natural rate of unemployment: the rate when cyclical unemployment is zero and output is at its normal level. Cyclical unemployment is the extra unemployment when aggregate demand is weak. It can be negative in a boom, when the actual rate falls below the natural rate and wage pressure tends to rise. The short-run Phillips curve summarises a trade-off at DSE level. For a given expected inflation rate, lower unemployment has often come with higher inflation, and higher unemployment with lower inflation. Treat that trade-off as short run. In the long run the curve is vertical at the natural rate. Trying to hold unemployment below the natural rate by raising demand does not permanently buy lower unemployment, because expected inflation catches up. Measurement can mislead. The CPI uses a fixed basket, so it can overstate the cost of living when households substitute toward goods that have become relatively cheaper, and it can miss quality improvements. The unemployment rate excludes discouraged workers, who have stopped searching and are outside the labour force, and it counts underemployed people as employed. A fall in the unemployment rate can therefore mean people left the labour force, not that more jobs were created. Hong Kong's official rates come from the General Household Survey.

example.scenario: Hong Kong's unemployment rate falls from 4.2% to 3.6%. Over the same quarter some hotel workers stop looking for work, the CPI basket still contains a brand of rice that many households have stopped buying, and a boom in logistics hiring pushes vacancies up.
example.walkthrough: Part of the fall in the unemployment rate may be a smaller labour force: discouraged hotel workers are no longer counted as unemployed, so the rate can fall without a matching rise in employment. Check the labour force and the number of employed persons before calling the figure a recovery. The fixed rice item is a CPI pitfall. If households switch to a cheaper rice, the fixed basket does not follow at once, so the index can overstate the rise in the cost of living. Logistics vacancies that suitable workers can fill after a short search are frictional. If the actual unemployment rate is below the natural rate, cyclical unemployment is negative and the short-run Phillips relation points to upward pressure on wages and prices. That pressure is not a permanent menu of lower unemployment at the same inflation rate. In the long run the Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate.

traps: Putting cyclical unemployment inside the natural rate. The natural rate is frictional plus structural unemployment.
Reading the short-run Phillips curve as a permanent policy menu. The long-run curve is vertical at the natural rate.
Treating a lower unemployment rate as proof that employment rose. People leaving the labour force can cut the rate.
Counting discouraged workers as unemployed. They are outside the labour force because they are not actively seeking work.
Assuming the CPI basket updates every time relative prices change. Substitution away from dearer goods is a reason the fixed basket can overstate the cost of living.

terms.definition: The unemployment rate when cyclical unemployment is zero. It is made up of frictional and structural unemployment.
A short-run inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation, drawn for a given expected inflation rate.
A vertical line at the natural rate of unemployment. There is no permanent trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
The tendency of a fixed-basket CPI to overstate the cost of living because households switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
A person who wants a job but has stopped searching, so is outside the labour force and not counted as unemployed.

L8.3.title: Deposit Creation: Numbers and Reserve-Ratio Pitfalls
L8.3.concept: Credit creation is easiest to see on a balance sheet. Suppose the required reserve ratio is 20% and a customer deposits $1,000 of cash that was previously outside the banks. The bank's reserves and deposits both rise by $1,000. Required reserves are $200, so excess reserves are $800. If the bank lends that $800 and the borrower spends it, the recipient's bank gains $800 of deposits and reserves. That bank keeps 20% and can lend the rest. With no cash drain and no extra reserves held idle, maximum total deposits equal the new reserves divided by the required reserve ratio: $1,000 / 0.20 = $5,000. Of that, $1,000 is the original deposit and $4,000 is created by lending. Several pitfalls break the textbook maximum. A cash drain means the public holds some of each loan as notes, so less is redeposited and the multiplier is smaller than 1/rrr. If banks hold excess reserves, they do not lend every dollar above the required ratio. The required reserve ratio is not the capital adequacy ratio: one is a fraction of deposits held as reserves, the other is capital against risk-weighted assets. In Hong Kong the statutory reserve ratio on Hong Kong dollar deposits is zero, and licensed banks still hold voluntary reserves for liquidity. The simple 1/rrr formula is a classroom model, not the operating rule of the currency board. Loan repayment destroys deposits, so the process also runs in reverse.

example.scenario: A customer deposits $1,000 in cash at a licensed bank. For this classroom example the required reserve ratio is 20%. There is no cash drain, and every bank lends out all excess reserves. Later the same customer repays a $800 loan in full.
example.walkthrough: Step 1: the cash deposit raises both deposits and reserves by $1,000. Step 2: required reserves are 0.20 times $1,000 = $200, so excess reserves are $800. Step 3: the first loan can be $800, not $1,000. The bank cannot lend the reserves it must keep. Step 4: if each later bank does the same, maximum total deposits are $1,000 / 0.20 = $5,000. Maximum new loans are $5,000 minus the original $1,000, which is $4,000. Step 5: if instead the public held part of each loan as cash, redeposits would be smaller and total deposits would stop short of $5,000. Step 6: when the $800 loan is repaid, that deposit is destroyed. Credit creation is not a one-way ratchet. None of these steps is the Hong Kong statutory ratio. On Hong Kong dollar deposits that ratio is zero, so this 20% figure is only a worked example of the formula.

traps: Lending the whole deposit. The first bank can lend only the excess over required reserves.
Calling $5,000 the amount of new loans. In this example $5,000 is maximum total deposits; new loans are $4,000.
Using 1/rrr when there is a cash drain or excess reserves. Both leakages make the actual multiplier smaller.
Confusing the required reserve ratio with the capital adequacy ratio. One is about reserves against deposits; the other is capital against risky assets.
Treating a textbook reserve ratio as Hong Kong's rule. The statutory ratio on HKD deposits is zero; banks hold voluntary reserves.

terms.definition: The fraction of deposits a bank must hold as reserves. In the simple model the deposit multiplier is 1 divided by this ratio.
In the simple model with no leakages, the maximum change in deposits divided by the change in reserves, equal to 1/rrr.
A leakage in which the public holds part of new loans as notes, so less is redeposited and the multiplier shrinks.
A solvency rule: capital as a fraction of risk-weighted assets. It is not the required reserve ratio.

L8.4.title: Excess Reserves and the Demand for Money
L8.4.concept: Banks hold excess reserves for their own reasons, not because the textbook multiplier says they must. Withdrawals are uncertain, so a reserve buffer reduces the chance of borrowing overnight or selling assets in a hurry. Loan demand may be weak, or borrowers may not look creditworthy. Liquidity rules and the need to settle payments also lead banks to keep balances they are not required to keep. If those balances sit idle, a cut in the required reserve ratio need not create the full textbook rise in deposits. In Hong Kong, where the statutory reserve ratio on Hong Kong dollar deposits is zero, the reserves banks actually hold are voluntary. Households and firms hold money for three motives that the HKDSE treatment usually names. The transactions motive is money kept to pay for planned purchases. It rises with income and with the number of payments, not mainly with the interest rate. The precautionary motive is money kept for unexpected payments. It also rises with income and with uncertainty. The speculative, or asset, motive is money held instead of interest-bearing assets such as bonds. When the interest rate rises, the opportunity cost of holding money rises, so speculative money demand falls. A rise in income shifts the money-demand curve right. A rise in the interest rate is a movement along the curve. People care about purchasing power, so a higher price level raises the nominal amount of money they wish to hold.

example.scenario: A licensed bank in Hong Kong keeps a large clearing balance even though it is not required to hold a fraction of HKD deposits as reserves. Over the same month household incomes rise, and the interest rate on Exchange Fund Bills rises.
example.walkthrough: The clearing balance is an excess, or voluntary, reserve. The bank may be guarding against withdrawals, waiting for better borrowers, or meeting its own liquidity needs. Because the statutory HKD reserve ratio is zero, this balance is not a required-reserve leftover from a 20% rule. It still limits lending: reserves that are not lent do not start a new round of deposits. For households, higher income raises transactions and precautionary demand, which shifts money demand to the right. The higher bill rate is different. It raises the opportunity cost of money, so speculative balances fall. That is a movement along the demand curve, not another shift from income. Do not read the bill rate as a freely chosen Hong Kong policy rate. Under the currency board, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are constrained by the link to the US dollar.

traps: Assuming banks lend every dollar above the required ratio. Excess reserves are a normal choice when withdrawals are uncertain or loan demand is weak.
Treating a rise in income as a movement along money demand. Income shifts the curve. The interest rate causes a movement along it.
Saying speculative money demand rises when the interest rate rises. A higher rate raises the opportunity cost of money, so speculative demand falls.
Calling Hong Kong banks' reserve balances a statutory HKD requirement. The statutory ratio on HKD deposits is zero; the balances are voluntary.
Confusing the demand for money with the demand for bonds. Bonds pay interest. Money is held despite that opportunity cost.

terms.definition: Reserves held above the required minimum, for withdrawals, weak loan demand, or liquidity. In Hong Kong, HKD reserve balances are voluntary because the statutory ratio is zero.
Holding money to make planned payments. It rises with income.
Holding money for unexpected payments. It rises with income and uncertainty.
Holding money instead of interest-bearing assets. It falls when the interest rate rises.
The interest given up by holding money rather than an interest-bearing asset.

L9.3.title: Crowding Out and Automatic Stabilisers
L9.3.concept: A rise in government spending raises aggregate demand, but the way a deficit is financed can offset part of that rise. If the government borrows in the loanable-funds market, the demand for funds increases and the interest rate tends to rise. Higher interest rates reduce interest-sensitive private investment and some spending on durables. That offset is crowding out. It is partial when spare capacity is large and private investment is not very sensitive to the interest rate. It is more complete when the economy is already near full employment, so extra demand mainly raises prices and interest rates rather than real output. Crowding out is not the same thing as a tax rise. Automatic stabilisers work without a new budget law. Under a progressive income tax, a boom raises tax revenue by more than income and a slump cuts tax revenue, so disposable income moves by less than pre-tax income. Unemployment benefits and similar transfers rise when people lose jobs and fall when they find work. That supports spending in a downturn and withdraws it in a boom. These movements change the budget balance by themselves: a recession can open a deficit even if nobody voted for a stimulus. A one-off cash handout is discretionary policy, not an automatic stabiliser, and it waits on recognition and implementation. In Hong Kong, fiscal reserves have been used as a buffer, so a deficit need not mean immediate large-scale borrowing. That limits one channel of crowding out. It does not remove the opportunity cost of using the reserves.

example.scenario: During a downturn the Hong Kong government pays more in unemployment-related support and collects less salaries tax, without passing a new stimulus bill. In a later year, near full employment, it borrows to fund a large new works programme.
example.walkthrough: The first year is the automatic stabilisers. Falling incomes cut salaries-tax payments under the existing schedule, and transfers rise because more people qualify. Disposable income falls by less than pre-tax income, so consumption falls by less than it otherwise would. No new ordinance is required. The budget moves toward deficit because revenue is down and transfers are up. The later works programme is discretionary. If it is financed by borrowing when the economy is already near full employment, the demand for loanable funds rises, interest rates tend to rise, and private investment is crowded out. Real output then rises by less than the simple multiplier suggests. Paying for the same programme from fiscal reserves avoids a new issue of debt, which weakens that interest-rate channel, but the reserves cannot be spent twice.

traps: Describing every deficit as a deliberate stimulus. A slump can cut tax revenue and raise transfers with no new law.
Ignoring financing. Borrowing can raise interest rates and crowd out private investment.
Saying crowding out is equally large in a deep recession and at full employment. It is stronger when there is little spare capacity.
Calling a one-off cash handout an automatic stabiliser. A handout is a discretionary decision.
Treating a transfer as government expenditure on goods and services. Transfers change disposable income; they are not themselves a G purchase in AD = C + I + G + X − M.

terms.definition: A fall in private investment, and some private spending, when government borrowing pushes up the interest rate.
A tax or transfer that changes with the cycle under existing rules and dampens swings in disposable income without a new policy decision.
A tax that takes a larger fraction of income as income rises, so revenue moves more than income over the cycle.
A deliberate change in spending or tax rates, such as a new public works vote or a one-off handout.
Accumulated government savings that can finance a deficit without immediate borrowing, limiting one channel of crowding out.

L9.4.title: Policy Lags and the Currency Board Limit
L9.4.concept: Policy does not hit the economy on the day a problem appears. The recognition lag is the time taken to see that output or inflation has changed, because data arrive late. The decision or implementation lag is the time taken to choose and carry out a response. For fiscal policy that often means a budget and legislation, so the lag can be long. A project that starts slowly may arrive after the recession has ended. The impact lag is the time from the policy action to its effect on spending and prices. Interest-rate changes often take many months to finish passing through mortgages, investment plans, and prices. These lags are a reason to avoid fine-tuning. Hong Kong faces a tighter constraint than a floating-rate central bank. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority operates a currency board under the Linked Exchange Rate System. The Hong Kong dollar is linked to the US dollar, and the Convertibility Undertakings keep the market rate inside a band of about 7.75 to 7.85 Hong Kong dollars per US dollar. The strong-side undertaking is 7.75. If the Hong Kong dollar is pushed to that strong rate, the HKMA buys US dollars from banks and sells Hong Kong dollars, which injects Hong Kong dollar liquidity. The weak-side undertaking is 7.85. If the Hong Kong dollar is pushed to that weak rate, the HKMA sells US dollars and buys Hong Kong dollars, which withdraws Hong Kong dollar liquidity. Because the monetary base is backed by US dollar reserves and the rate is held inside that band, Hong Kong does not run an independent monetary policy. Local interest rates tend to follow US rates. If the United States tightens while Hong Kong is weak, the HKMA cannot cut the Base Rate on its own to stimulate demand without undermining the undertaking. Fiscal policy and the fiscal reserves are the main local stabilisation tools.

example.scenario: The US Federal Reserve is raising the Fed Funds rate. Hong Kong retail sales are weak. The Hong Kong dollar is trading near 7.85 per US dollar, and a proposed public-works vote will not pass for several months.
example.walkthrough: Near 7.85 the Hong Kong dollar is at the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, not the strong side. The strong side is 7.75. At 7.85 the HKMA sells US dollars and buys Hong Kong dollars, withdrawing HKD liquidity. It does not buy US dollars at 7.85, and it does not move the weak side to 7.75. Cutting the Base Rate while the US rate is rising would work against that undertaking, so the HKMA does not have a free interest-rate policy of the kind a floating-rate central bank has. The weak retail sales are a local reason one might want easier money, but the currency board imports US monetary conditions. The works vote is fiscal policy. The months before it passes are an implementation lag. Even after the vote, spending and jobs respond with an impact lag. A project that arrives after the slump can add demand when it is no longer needed. The local tool that remains available is fiscal policy, including the use of fiscal reserves, not an independent monetary easing.

traps: Reversing the Convertibility Undertakings. Strong side is 7.75, where the HKMA buys USD and sells HKD. Weak side is 7.85, where the HKMA sells USD and buys HKD.
Saying the HKMA can set the Base Rate independently of the US Federal Reserve. Under the currency board, Hong Kong does not run an independent monetary policy.
Describing 7.80 as an interest rate. The link is an exchange rate of Hong Kong dollars per US dollar. The convertibility zone is about 7.75 to 7.85.
Ignoring lags. A correctly aimed stimulus can arrive after the economy has already turned.
Treating a long impact lag as a reason to change the peg. The lag is about how slowly spending responds. It does not free the HKMA to float the currency.

terms.definition: The delay before policymakers can see, from the data, that output or inflation has changed.
The delay between recognising a problem and putting a policy into effect. It is often long for fiscal decisions that need legislation.
The delay between a policy action and its full effect on spending, output, and prices.
The HKMA's commitment at the edges of the band: buy USD at the strong side of 7.75, and sell USD at the weak side of 7.85.

A system in which the monetary base is backed by foreign reserves and the domestic currency is linked to an anchor currency. Hong Kong's board links the HKD to the USD, so monetary policy is not independent.

L1.5.title: Chart trap: movement along a curve versus a shift
L1.5.concept: Most lost marks on a demand-and-supply diagram come from moving the wrong object. A change in the price of the good itself is a movement along the demand or supply curve. The curve is the whole relationship; one price picks one point on it. A change in anything else that the model is holding constant shifts the curve. For demand, that includes income, tastes, the price of a related good, and expectations. For supply, it includes input prices, technology, and the number of sellers. When two things happen together, separate them before you draw. A higher own-price and a fall in income are not two shifts. Draw the income shift, then read the new quantity at the new price, or compare equilibria after the shift only. Label the axes: price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis. State whether price and quantity rise, fall, or are ambiguous. If demand and supply both shift, one of price or quantity is usually ambiguous unless you know which shift is larger. Say so, instead of inventing a direction.

example.scenario: The price of coffee rises. At the same time, a report says tea and coffee are substitutes, and the price of tea has also risen.
example.walkthrough: The coffee price rise, by itself, is a movement along the coffee demand curve. The tea price rise is a different event: tea and coffee are substitutes, so demand for coffee shifts right. On the finished diagram the demand curve has moved, and equilibrium price and quantity of coffee are higher than they would have been from the supply side alone. Do not also shift supply unless an input or technology fact is given.

traps: Saying demand falls when the own price rises. That is a fall in quantity demanded.
Shifting both curves because two numbers changed, without asking which variable each number is.
Leaving price and quantity both ‘up’ when the two shifts push them in opposite directions.

terms.definition: A change in quantity demanded or supplied caused only by the good’s own price.
A new curve, caused by a determinant other than the good’s own price.
When two shifts have opposite effects on price or on quantity, so the diagram does not decide the direction without more information.

L2.4.title: Elasticity traps: sign, base, and the straight-line curve
L2.4.concept: Elasticity is a ratio of percentage changes, not a slope. Slope can be constant while elasticity changes. On a straight-line demand curve, absolute price elasticity is high at the top, equal to one at the midpoint, and low at the bottom. Classify demand with the absolute value. The negative sign of PED only repeats the law of demand. Income elasticity keeps its sign: positive for normal goods, negative for inferior goods. When you calculate a percentage, say which base you use. A change from 100 to 80 is 20% of the original quantity. Mixing the new value into the base without saying so will not match the mark scheme’s figure. For tax questions, compare elasticities rather than memorising that buyers always pay. The more inelastic side of the market bears more of a per-unit tax. Perfectly inelastic demand means buyers bear the whole tax. Time matters for supply: short-run PES is usually lower because some inputs are fixed.

example.scenario: Price rises from $20 to $25 and quantity demanded falls from 40 to 30. A classmate says PED is 0.5 because the curve looks flat, and also says the good is inferior because PED is negative.
example.walkthrough: Percentage change in quantity is 10/40 = 25%. Percentage change in price is 5/20 = 25%. |PED| = 1. The slope of the drawing is not the elasticity. The minus sign does not make the good inferior. Inferior is a negative income elasticity, which this price change does not measure.

traps: Treating a constant slope as a constant elasticity.
Calling demand inelastic because PED is negative.
Using income elasticity language (inferior, normal) for a price elasticity result.

terms.definition: PED without the minus sign. Greater than 1 is elastic demand.
Absolute price elasticity equal to 1. Total spending by buyers stays the same when price changes, for that small move.
How the burden of a tax is split. It follows relative elasticities, not the side the law says must send the cheque.

L3.4.title: Chart trap: ceiling, floor, tax wedge, and deadweight loss
L3.4.concept: Draw the free-market equilibrium first, then add the intervention. A price ceiling is a horizontal line. It binds only below equilibrium, and then quantity supplied is less than quantity demanded: a shortage. A price floor binds only above equilibrium, and then there is a surplus. A non-binding control should be drawn, labelled, and then ignored in the result. A per-unit tax drives a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers keep. Shift the supply curve up by the tax, or mark the two prices with a vertical gap equal to the tax. The quantity is where the new supply meets demand. Consumer surplus and producer surplus shrink. The rectangle between the two prices, up to the new quantity, is tax revenue, a transfer. The triangle beside it, from the new quantity out to the old equilibrium, is deadweight loss: units no longer traded even though buyers valued them above the sellers’ cost. Do not shade revenue and call it the loss.

example.scenario: Equilibrium rent is $12,000. The government sets a ceiling of $14,000 and asks what shortage appears.
example.walkthrough: The ceiling is above equilibrium, so it does not bind. Rent stays $12,000 and there is no shortage. If the ceiling were $10,000, you would read quantity demanded and quantity supplied at $10,000 and subtract. The shortage is that gap, not the distance between $12,000 and $10,000 in dollars.

traps: Drawing a shortage under a price floor, or a surplus under a binding ceiling.
Counting tax revenue as deadweight loss.
Applying a non-binding ceiling as if it changed the price.

terms.definition: A price control that stops the market reaching equilibrium. A ceiling binds below equilibrium; a floor binds above it.
The gap between the price paid by buyers and the price received by sellers, equal to the per-unit tax.
The total surplus lost because some worthwhile trades do not happen.

L4.4.title: Chart trap: MC, AVC, ATC, and economic cost
L4.4.concept: Marginal cost cuts both AVC and ATC at their minimum points. That is because the marginal pulls the average down when it is below the average, and pulls it up when it is above. A change in fixed cost shifts ATC and AFC, not MC and not AVC. A change in a variable input price shifts MC, AVC, and ATC. Diminishing marginal returns is the short-run reason MC eventually rises: one input is fixed, so extra units of the variable input add less output and cost more at the margin. Economies of scale are different. They are long-run, when all inputs can change, and they show up as a falling long-run average cost. Economic cost includes implicit opportunity cost. A owner-manager’s forgone wage and the forgone rent on her own shop are real costs even though no invoice exists. Positive accounting profit can sit next to negative economic profit. Shutdown is a separate short-run test: if price is below AVC, the firm loses less by stopping production.

example.scenario: A firm’s rent rises. A student shifts the marginal-cost curve up and says profit-maximising output must change.
example.walkthrough: Rent is a fixed cost if it does not vary with output. MC is unchanged, so the output where MR = MC is unchanged. ATC shifts up, so profit falls. If the firm is a price taker, price did not change. Only if the higher ATC means price is now below AVC — which a fixed-cost rise does not do — would shutdown be the issue.

traps: Shifting MC when only fixed cost changes.
Calling diminishing returns a long-run economies-of-scale result.
Using accounting profit as if it already included opportunity cost.

terms.definition: The extra cost of one more unit. It ignores fixed cost that does not change with that unit.
An opportunity cost with no cash payment, included in economic cost.
The output where MC crosses ATC. Producing there is productively efficient for that plant.

L5.4.title: Chart trap: the firm’s demand, MR, and long-run profit
L5.4.concept: Start every structure question by drawing the demand curve the firm itself faces. In perfect competition that line is horizontal at the market price, so price, average revenue, and marginal revenue are the same. In monopoly and monopolistic competition the firm’s demand slopes down. For a single-price firm, marginal revenue then lies below demand, because a price cut applies to all units. Profit-maximising output is where MR = MC, provided price covers AVC in the short run. Price is read from demand, not from the MR = MC crossing. In the long run, free entry pushes a perfectly competitive firm to zero economic profit: the horizontal demand is tangent to ATC at its minimum. A monopoly can keep economic profit if entry is blocked. Do not draw a competitive firm with a downward-sloping demand, and do not set monopoly output where P = MC unless the question asks for the efficient quantity rather than the chosen quantity.

example.scenario: A price-taking noodle shop sees the market price fall. The student shades a loss and says the shop must be a monopoly because it is making a loss.
example.walkthrough: Losses happen in perfect competition in the short run if price is below ATC. The shop is still a price taker if it cannot affect the market price. Check AVC. If price is above AVC, it keeps producing where P = MC. If free entry and exit are at work, long-run losses drive exit until price returns to minimum ATC. A loss is not evidence of monopoly.

traps: Setting monopoly output where the demand curve crosses MC.
Drawing MR equal to price for a single-price monopolist.
Treating a short-run loss as proof that the market is not competitive.

terms.definition: A firm that sells any quantity at the market price and none above it.
A monopolist that charges the same price for every unit, so MR is below demand.
Revenue covers explicit and implicit costs. It is the long-run result of free entry, not a signal to shut down.

L6.4.title: Chart and definition trap: nominal GDP, real GDP, and what is left out
L6.4.concept: Nominal GDP values current output at current prices. Real GDP values output at the prices of a base year, so a rise means quantities have risen, not merely prices. If a question gives both a nominal change and an inflation rate, do not award the whole nominal change to output. GDP counts final goods and services produced inside the territory. Intermediate goods are left out to avoid double counting, or they are captured inside the value of the final good. Transfer payments such as a cash allowance with nothing produced in return are not GDP. A teacher’s salary is different: a service is produced. GDP is location; GNP adjusts for net income from abroad and follows ownership. The expenditure identity is C + I + G + X − M. Imports are removed because they were included in the other spending but not produced at home. Even a correct real-GDP rise is not a full welfare result. It misses unpaid work, the distribution of income, and many environmental costs. Say that limit when the question asks whether people are better off.

example.scenario: Nominal GDP rises 6% and the GDP deflator rises 6%. A commentary says the economy produced 6% more goods.
example.walkthrough: Prices account for the whole 6%. Real GDP is roughly unchanged. The commentary confused nominal with real. If the question also mentions a rise in elderly allowances, that transfer is not an extra component of GDP on top of government spending on goods and services.

traps: Reading a nominal increase as a real increase.
Adding transfer payments into GDP.
Treating a real-GDP rise as proof that every household gained.

terms.definition: Output valued at current prices. It changes when prices change, even if quantities do not.
Output valued at base-year prices, used to compare quantities over time.
A payment for which no good or service is produced in return. It is not part of GDP.

econ-u01-mischart.title: Chart trap: movement along a curve versus a shift
econ-u01-mischart.concept: A change in the good's own price moves you along the curve: quantity demanded or quantity supplied changes, the curve does not move. A change in a non-price determinant moves the whole curve. Demand shifts for income, tastes, related-goods prices, expectations and the number of buyers. Supply shifts for input costs, technology, taxes and subsidies, expectations and the number of sellers. Label both axes P and Q, mark the original Pe and Qe, and use arrows differently: a slide is shown along one curve, a shift is shown as a second curve with an arrow between them.

example.scenario: The government raises the minimum wage, and a cafe's hourly wage bill rises at the same time as demand for takeaway coffee falls because a new rival opens nearby.
example.walkthrough: The higher wage is an input cost, so it shifts the cafe's supply curve left or up. The rival's effect is a non-price change in demand, so the demand curve shifts left. Neither is a movement along a curve, because neither is a change in the cafe's own price. Mark the new intersection and compare it with the old Pe and Qe.

traps: Calling a slide along the demand curve an increase in demand.
Shifting supply when only buyers' income changed.
Forgetting to state ceteris paribus before interpreting a change.

terms.definition: All other determinants of demand or supply held constant while one is changed.
The quantity demanded that rises when price falls; a movement along the demand curve.
A rightward shift of the whole demand curve caused by a non-price factor.

econ-u02-mischart.title: Chart trap: elasticity on the straight-line demand curve
econ-u02-mischart.concept: PED is a ratio of percentage changes, not a slope. State the base you use, or use the midpoint method, and keep the signs. On a straight-line demand curve the slope is constant but |PED| falls as you move down the curve, because P x Q is constant while P over Q rises. The revenue test is a quick check: if price falls and total revenue rises, that range is elastic. YED is positive for normal goods and negative for inferior goods; XED is positive for substitutes and negative for complements; PES depends on the time period available.

example.scenario: A cafe cuts its coffee price by 10% and total revenue for the week rises by 4%.
example.walkthrough: Price down with revenue up means the percentage rise in quantity exceeded the 10% fall in price, so demand is elastic in that range. If asked for the PED value you still need the percentage change in quantity; if asked only to classify, the revenue evidence is enough.

traps: Treating the slope of the demand curve as the PED.
Dropping the sign story when the question asks about YED or XED.
Using the PED formula with the percentage changes swapped.

terms.definition: A percentage change computed from the average of the old and new values.
Price and revenue moving in opposite directions indicates elastic or inelastic demand.
The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income.

econ-u03-mischart.title: Chart trap: ceiling, floor, tax wedge and deadweight loss
econ-u03-mischart.concept: Draw the free-market equilibrium first, then add the intervention. A binding ceiling is a horizontal line below Pe and creates shortage; a binding floor is a horizontal line above Pe and creates surplus. A per-unit tax creates a vertical wedge of width equal to the tax between the price buyers pay and the price sellers keep, and it shrinks the traded quantity. The deadweight loss is the triangle of mutually beneficial trades that no longer happen. Tax incidence follows the elasticities of the two sides, not the name on the statute.

example.scenario: A city caps the rent of a small flat below the market equilibrium rent and also puts a fixed tax on each property transaction.
example.walkthrough: The cap is binding only if it sits below Pe; it creates shortage and queues, and a black market or lower quality can appear. The transaction tax shifts supply up by the tax and draws a wedge between the buyer's price and the seller's net price. In each case shade the change in consumer and producer surplus and label the lost triangle.

traps: Drawing a ceiling above Pe and still calling it binding.
Claiming the statutory payer always bears the whole tax.
Shading the consumer and producer surplus triangles on the wrong side of the wedge.

terms.definition: A control that changes the market outcome because it is set on the effective side of equilibrium.
The vertical distance between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive, equal to the per-unit tax.
The surplus lost from trades that are beneficial to both sides but no longer take place.

econ-u04-mischart.title: Chart trap: MC, AVC, ATC and economic cost
econ-u04-mischart.concept: Marginal cost is the change in total cost, or in total variable cost in the short run, from one more unit. Average fixed cost is total fixed cost divided by output and falls continuously. ATC = AVC + AFC, so ATC sits above AVC with a gap that narrows as output rises. The MC curve cuts both AVC and ATC at their minimum points because the marginal pulls an average down when it is below it and up when it is above it. Economic cost adds the opportunity cost of owner-supplied factors to explicit cost, so accounting profit overstates economic profit.

example.scenario: A bakery records total fixed cost of $12,000 a month and variable cost of $30,000 for 3,000 loaves, then raises output to 4,000 loaves with total variable cost $38,000.
example.walkthrough: AFC falls from $4 to $3 a loaf. AVC rises from $10 to $9.50, so AVC is already turning up, which tells you the bakery is past its efficient short-run scale. Compare ATC of $14 with $12.50 and check where the MC of the extra 1,000 loaves, $8 a loaf, sits relative to each average.

traps: Claiming MC always equals ATC.
Judging profit without the owner's implicit cost.
Drawing AFC rising with output.

terms.definition: The extra cost of producing one more unit in the relevant period.
Total cost divided by output, equal to AVC plus AFC.
The opportunity cost of resources the owner supplies without a separate invoice.

econ-u05-mischart.title: Chart trap: the firm's own demand, MR and long-run profit
econ-u05-mischart.concept: Start every structure question with the demand curve the firm itself faces. Under perfect competition it is horizontal at the market price, so P = MR and profit is (P - ATC) x Q. Under a downward-sloping firm demand, MR lies below P because a price cut applies to every unit sold. Choose output where MR = MC, then read the price off the demand curve; never set P = MC for a monopoly as the private optimum. In the long run, free entry pushes perfect competition and monopolistic competition to normal profit, while a monopoly can keep supernormal profit only because entry is blocked.

example.scenario: A local bus company faces a downward-sloping demand curve and is considering a rival's entry.
example.walkthrough: Sketch the bus firm's demand and the MR curve below it, add the cost curves, and mark output where MR = MC. Read the price from the demand curve, compare it with ATC to get profit per bus, then multiply by the number of buses. Note that entry would move the firm towards normal profit, which is why the incumbent may resist it.

traps: Setting P = MC for a monopoly as the profit-maximising condition.
Claiming monopolistic competition always earns long-run supernormal profit.
Forgetting to read the price from the demand curve after MR = MC.

terms.definition: The extra revenue from selling one more unit, which falls faster than price on a downward-sloping demand curve.
Profit above the normal return, possible only when entry is restricted.
Charging different prices for the same product in ways that are not cost-justified.

econ-u06-mischart.title: Chart trap: nominal against real GDP, and what AD includes
econ-u06-mischart.concept: Nominal GDP values current output at current prices, so it can rise because prices rose. Real GDP holds prices at a base year, so it tracks volume; the gap between the two is the price effect, measured by the GDP deflator. Aggregate demand is C + I + G + (X - M); imports are subtracted because they are spending on foreign output. Name the inflation type from the diagram: demand-pull comes from AD shifting right along SRAS, cost-push from SRAS shifting left, and the two give different short-run output effects.

example.scenario: Nominal GDP rises 4% in a year in which the GDP deflator rises 3%, and the country also imports more components for local assembly.
example.walkthrough: Real growth is roughly 4% minus 3%, about 1%, so most of the nominal rise was prices. The extra imports reduce net exports, so they subtract from aggregate demand even though they look like activity in the trade figures. On an AD-SRAS diagram the price rise alone is not evidence of demand-pull inflation.

traps: Reading a rise in nominal GDP as a rise in output.
Adding imports into aggregate demand instead of subtracting them.
Calling any CPI rise demand-pull without a diagram to justify it.

terms.definition: The ratio of nominal GDP to real GDP, showing the price effect on output.
Inflation caused by rising production costs, shifting SRAS left.
A component of spending, such as imports or saving, that leaves the circular flow.
